extracted.intended_audience: editors, writers, copyeditors, and publishers using the Chicago Manual of Style
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and conventions from the Chicago Manual of Style for forming, punctuating, and using abbreviations, symbols, units, and related conventions in running text, addresses, tables, notes, and scholarly apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with states/provinces in text and addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: States, provinces, and territories are enclosed in commas in running text and addresses except where specifically noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enclose a state/province in commas when it follows a city in running text (e.g., Bedford, PA, and Jamestown, NY). Exception: no comma appears between the postal code and a zip code. See related rules (10.31, 10.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating geographic generic terms (Fort, Mount, Saint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic terms in geographic names are usually spelled out in formal prose but may be abbreviated when space is limited or usage warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of acceptable abbreviations: Fort (Ft.), Mount (Mt.), Saint (St.). Do not abbreviate San and Santa (e.g., San Diego, Santa Barbara). For French place-names with Saint consult the French guidance (see 11.26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating country names
rubrics_metrics.description: Country names are usually spelled out in running text but may be abbreviated in tables, lists, and similar compact formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discretion forming abbreviations; for tables define any abbreviation in a note to avoid confusion. Initialisms (UAE, US, UK) may be used in running text after the full form has been established. For technical lists consider ISO 3166-1 alpha-2/alpha-3 codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: "US" versus "United States" usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional editorial practice spelled out 'United States' as a noun and used 'US' for the adjective; Chicago now permits using 'US' as a noun subject to editorial discretion when meaning is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred traditional forms: 'United States' (noun), 'US' (adjective) — e.g., 'US dollars', 'US involvement in China' vs 'China's involvement in the United States' or 'China's involvement in the US'. See related guidance 10.3 and 10.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailing-address abbreviations: postal vs. standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the U.S. Postal Service standard (all caps, no periods) for mailing addresses; Chicago prefers a different (period-using) style for tabular matter and similar contexts; spell out in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPS forms (e.g., AVE, PO BOX) are appropriate for mailing; in tables Chicago prefers forms like Ave., Bldg., Rd.; in running text spell out street designators. Consult USPS for postal abbreviations and dictionaries for other forms (see 10.34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compass-point abbreviations in mailing addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-letter compass points accompanying a street name are normally followed by a period; two-letter compass points are not; NE, NW, SE, SW remain abbreviated even in running text when used in addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1060 E. Prospect Ave. (or in running text, 1060 East Prospect Avenue); 456 NW Lane St. (or in running text, 456 NW Lane Street). The USPS omits periods; follow USPS on mailings (see 10.34–10.36).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abbreviate compass points when they are part of a name
rubrics_metrics.description: If a compass point is the name or part of the name of a street or place-name, it must be spelled out (not abbreviated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abbreviate in names such as South Ave., Northwest Hwy., South Shore Dr., West Bend, East Orange — spell the compass element out as part of the proper name (see 10.36).

rubrics_metrics.name: General compass-point abbreviations outside addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of the compass may be abbreviated (N, E, S, W, NE, SE, etc.), usually without periods, but in formal nontechnical prose these terms are usually spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer or technical compass abbreviations (NNE, ENE, etc.) are acceptable in technical contexts; in formal narrative prefer spelled-out directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latitude and longitude abbreviation and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In nontechnical contexts, 'latitude' and 'longitude' are not abbreviated; in technical contexts lat and long (or lat/long) may be used; coordinates can be expressed in several equivalent formats and primes/double primes are used for minutes/seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of equivalent forms: N 36 25.217, W 44 23.017 = 36°25'13" N, 44°23'01" W. Use primes (') and double primes (") for minutes and seconds, not quotation marks. In technical coordinates 'lat 42°15'09" N, long 89°17'45" W' is acceptable (see 10.36).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological-era abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use uppercase era abbreviations with no periods (e.g., AD, BC, BCE, CE) and follow conventions for placement relative to year numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally these appeared in small capitals with periods; Chicago recommends full capitals without periods. Some precede the year (AD) while others follow it (BCE). See also 9.34 for date-numbering guidance (10.41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Month and day abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When space requires abbreviating months or days, Chicago recommends certain abbreviated forms (typically with periods) for formal prose, while computer/indexing systems may use period-less variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Month example (formal prose preferred): Jan., Feb., Mar., Apr., etc. Alternative systems without periods (Jan, Feb, Mar) are common in computer contexts and indexes. Day example (formal prose): Sun., Mon., Tues., Wed., Thurs., Fri., Sat.; alternative compact forms (Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat) exist for different contexts (see 10.41–10.42).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-of-day abbreviations and usage (a.m./p.m.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a.m. and p.m. in lowercase with periods for times of day; do not combine a.m./p.m. with words like 'morning' or 'afternoon'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred forms: 10:30 a.m. or 'ten thirty in the morning' (spelled-out alternative). Time zones, when needed, are usually given in parentheses (e.g., 4:45 p.m. (CST)). Note that UTC has largely superseded GMT, but GMT remains in common use (see 10.41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly abbreviations placement and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly abbreviations and symbols (especially Latin and bibliographic abbreviations) are typically confined to parentheses or notes in formal prose; choose longer forms when in doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many Latin abbreviations are set in roman; complete Latin words like 'ab', 'ad', 'et' take no periods. If multiple abbreviation choices exist (e.g., 'L.' vs 'Lat.' for Latin), the choice depends on preference, context, and readership; when unsure, use the longer form (see 10.42).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard scholarly abbreviations and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conventional scholarly abbreviations and symbols in bibliographies, glossaries, and scholarly apparatus; some are retained mainly to interpret older texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include abbr. (abbreviated), ed. (editor/edition), f. (folio), ibid. (ibidem), id. (idem), et al., etc. Guidance also notes style choices like 'ed.' vs 'edited by' and advises not adding 'by' after 'ed.' (see 10.42–10.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biblical-book names in running text vs citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out books of the Bible in running text; use standard abbreviations in parenthetical citations, notes, or where many references appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'According to Genesis 1:27, ...' For a concordance or many references, abbreviations are appropriate: Gen. 47:12, Ruth 4:15, etc. See the lists of OT/NT abbreviations provided (10.45–10.48) and consult SBL Handbook for specialized cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviating Bible versions and sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Versions and sections of the Bible are usually abbreviated as initialisms (e.g., RSV, NRSV, AV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common abbreviations: RSV (Revised Standard Version), NRSV (New Revised Standard Version), AV (Authorized Version/King James), OT, NT, LXX, MT, etc. Use the conventional initialism appropriate to the edition (10.48).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and scientific abbreviations—periods, capitalization, spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical and scientific contexts, periods are omitted from abbreviations/symbols for units; capitalization follows current usage (proper-name-derived units capitalized), and a space usually appears between a numeral and unit symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 22 m (not 22 m.), 36°C (no space before °C in Chicago style though SI guidance differs). Capitalize unit symbols derived from proper names (A, V) but not unit names when spelled out. Plurals do not add periods or change the symbol (10 A, 5 ha). Consult SI and Scientific Style and Format for detailed cases (10.49, 10.52–10.59).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical abbreviations formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical abbreviations commonly used in tables and statistical material are often italicized and follow conventional short forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common items include ANCOVA, ANOVA, CI (confidence interval), df (degrees of freedom), IQR (interquartile range), MLE, MS, sd/SD, se/SE, etc. See table guidance (12.57–12.58) and table 12.3 for usage conventions (10.50).

rubrics_metrics.name: SI units: symbols, plurals, base units, and prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: SI symbols have no periods, use the same symbol for singular and plural, and are mostly lowercase except for those derived from proper names; apply prefixes for multiples/submultiples and use the standardized prefix symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base units: meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd). Prefixes (k, M, G, m, µ, n, etc.) form multiples/submultiples (km, ms). Use spaces between numeral and unit (22 m), except noted exceptions in SI practice; avoid using prefixes to denote binary powers—use kibi (Ki), mebi (Mi), gibi (Gi), etc., when binary multiples are required (10.51–10.57).

rubrics_metrics.name: SI-derived units, spacing, and numerical range guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived units have standard symbols and can be expressed algebraically in base units; only numbers between 0.1 and 1,000 should be expressed in the base unit without using a multiple (prefer using a suitable prefix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express 12,000 meters as 12 km (not 12,000 m) and 0.003 cm3 as 3 mm3 (not 0.003 cm3). SI practice usually uses a space between number and unit; SI also recommends a space before % and degree symbol, though Chicago does not require those exceptions (10.58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-SI units accepted for use
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain widely used non-SI units are accepted within SI usage, with Chicago-specific capitalization or forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: liter (L — capitalized to avoid confusion with the numeral 1), metric ton (t), hour (h). Chicago notes these as accepted even though not officially SI (10.58–10.59).

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical coordinate and abbreviation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Celestial coordinates use right ascension (RA or a) in hours/minutes/seconds and declination (Dec or δ) in degrees/minutes/seconds, with appropriate symbols and superscripts as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format example: 14h 6m 7s, −49° 8' 22". Decimal fractions and abbreviated indicators (AU, pc, kpc, Mpc, UT) follow the specialized astronomical conventions; consult IAU guidance for detailed cases (10.63).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical element names and symbols conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Element names are lowercase; symbols have an initial capital; names for undiscovered/temporary elements may use Latin-based provisional names; symbols and names use no periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow IUPAC-approved names and symbols (e.g., Al for aluminum/aluminium, Sb for antimony [stibium]); use provisional Latin-based temporary names for unconfirmed elements (e.g., ununoctium historically). No periods after symbols; symbols are capitalized as required (10.63).
